case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Hawaii’s restrictions on the public carrying of firearms violate the Second Amendment under the text-and-history test mandated by Bruen, and whether courts may rely on party-retained “experts” to supply what are effectively legal conclusions about founding-era law.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. II (as incorporated against the States through the Fourteenth Amendment); governing evidentiary framework referenced: Fed. R. Evid. 702 (scope of expert testimony).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that the Second Amendment’s plain text covers their proposed conduct (carrying arms for self-defense), triggering a presumption of protection under Bruen. They contend Hawaii cannot meet its burden to identify a well-established historical analogue supporting the modern restrictions, and that generalized public-safety or empirical-policy justifications are insufficient after Heller/McDonald/Bruen. They further argue that Hawaii’s use of historians as “experts” improperly offers legal conclusions (how courts should interpret founding-era statutes and constitutional meaning), which should be excluded under Rule 702 because statutory and constitutional interpretation is the court’s job, not expert testimony.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent (Hawaii) maintains its public-carry regime is consistent with the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation, asserting that historical sources—properly understood—show governments long regulated the manner, locations, and conditions of bearing arms to promote public safety. Hawaii’s approach relies on historical interpretations to argue that the Second Amendment right is not unlimited and that modern public-carry restrictions fall within historically recognized regulatory authority. Hawaii also appears to defend the use of historians and historical testimony to explain the historical record and to support its claimed analogues (even as petitioners characterize that testimony as crossing into impermissible legal argument).
key_precedents: District of Columbia v. Heller, 554 U.S. 570 (2008)
McDonald v. City of Chicago, 561 U.S. 742 (2010)
New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n, Inc. v. Bruen, 597 U.S. 1 (2022)
Commodores Entertainment Corp. v. McClary, 879 F.3d 1114 (11th Cir. 2018)
United States v. Herring, 955 F.2d 703 (11th Cir. 1992)
Heller v. District of Columbia, 670 F.3d 1244 (D.C. Cir. 2011) (Kavanaugh, J., dissenting) (as quoted)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that Heller and Bruen preserve meaningful, historically grounded regulation of manner and truly “sensitive places”—is correct, and it counsels against any categorical pronouncement that States can never regulate locations or private property. But Justice Thomas is also right that Bruen forbids validating a regime by appealing to regulation at a high level of generality; if Hawaii’s default rule (especially the private-property presumption) functionally bars carry in most ordinary places absent affirmative consent, that looks like a near-prohibition and demands a well-established, representative historical analogue with a comparable burden and justification. Consistent with Justice Kavanaugh’s administrability concerns and my own institutional-minimalism, the proper course is a narrow holding keyed to the law’s real-world operation and the State’s failure (on this record) to supply concrete analogues—while clarifying, as Justice Kagan notes, that Rule 702 may provide historical context and authentication but cannot outsource the court’s constitutional analogue-matching duty to experts. On that basis, I remain with Petitioner while leaving room for genuinely historical, limited sensitive-place and manner regulations.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that Heller and Bruen acknowledge the right is “not unlimited” and permit regulation of manner and “sensitive places,” but that principle cannot be used to justify a default rule that forbids carrying on most private property open to the public absent affirmative consent—an approach that functionally nullifies the right to “bear Arms” rather than regulates its exercise. Under Bruen, Hawaii must identify a well-established, representative founding-era analogue imposing a comparably broad prohibition; abstract invocations of historical “regulation” are insufficient, and public-safety stakes cannot reintroduce interest balancing through the back door. I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch that Rule 702 may allow historians to supply context and authenticate sources, but it cannot permit party-retained experts to deliver ultimate constitutional or statutory interpretations that displace the court’s duty to determine original public meaning and assess analogical fit. Because the State’s proffered tradition appears to rest on overgeneralized categories rather than concrete, comparable historical restrictions, the regime is inconsistent with the Second Amendment as understood in Heller, McDonald, and Bruen.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that Heller and Bruen preserve historically grounded regulation of manner and truly “sensitive places”—is correct, but it operates at too high a level of generality and does not satisfy Bruen’s requirement that the State produce a well-established, representative analogue imposing a comparable burden for a comparable reason. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, we must look to the law’s practical operation; a default rule that makes carry depend on affirmative private consent and sweeps across ordinary places open to the public functions less like a regulation and more like a near-prohibition, which history must specifically justify. Justice Jackson’s suggestion of granular preservation of historically tethered components may be appropriate as a remedial matter, but it cannot save a statutory design whose core presumption appears to nullify the right absent concrete analogues. On Rule 702, I agree with Roberts and Thomas that historians can provide context and authenticate sources, but courts cannot outsource the analogue-matching and constitutional meaning to experts.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s “license to carry nowhere” critique squarely raises the best point for Petitioners: if Hawaii’s private-property presumption and location bans, in actual operation, leave ordinary, law-abiding citizens with no meaningful places to carry, Bruen’s protection of public carry is effectively nullified. But Chief Justice Roberts’s own emphasis on a narrow, operation-focused inquiry supports my view that the right remedy is not a categorical invalidation of the entire regime; under Heller and Bruen, the State can still justify genuinely sensitive-place restrictions and historically grounded manner rules, and courts must separate those from any overbroad applications that function as a near-total ban. Justice Kagan is also right that courts—not experts under Rule 702—must do the analogical matching, which further counsels a granular, court-driven assessment of each challenged provision’s burden and historical comparability rather than an all-or-nothing facial judgment. On this record, Petitioners have shown serious overbreadth concerns, but not that every component lacks a representative analogue or that a targeted remedy cannot preserve meaningful avenues for carry consistent with Bruen.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point—that Heller and Bruen preserve historically grounded regulation of manner and genuinely “sensitive places”—is correct, but it does not carry the State’s burden under Bruen to produce a well-established, representative analogue with a comparable burden and justification for a default regime that, in operation, makes ordinary public carry exceptional. Justice Jackson’s call for a granular, provision-by-provision approach is methodologically appealing, yet it cannot rescue provisions whose design effectively flips Bruen’s presumption by banning carry across most everyday places absent affirmative consent; that kind of breadth requires concrete historical matches, not generalized invocations of “regulation.” I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that Rule 702 can admit historians for context and authentication, but not for bottom-line constitutional conclusions—otherwise the analogue inquiry becomes expert-driven and risks drifting back into interest balancing that Bruen rejected. Nothing in the Respondents’ arguments identifies the necessary historically comparable prohibitions, so I remain with the Petitioner.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point—that Heller and Bruen allow historically grounded regulation of manner and truly sensitive places—does not, on my methodology, satisfy Bruen’s allocation of the burden: Hawaii must identify a well-established, representative analogue matching the law’s “how and why,” not rely on regulatory tradition at a high level of abstraction. Justice Jackson’s suggestion of a granular, component-by-component salvaging would be plausible only if the State carried that burden for each materially burdensome feature; on this record, the private-property default and broad location restrictions appear to function as the sort of “carry nowhere” regime Justice Thomas warns against, and judicial narrowing cannot supply the missing history. I also agree with Chief Justice Roberts that Rule 702 may admit historians for context and authentication, but we cannot outsource the constitutional analogue judgment to experts or let that become a vehicle for interest balancing. Nothing raised in conference undermines the conclusion that the statute, as enacted and operating in practice, fails Bruen’s required historical showing.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point—that Heller and Bruen allow historically grounded manner regulations and genuinely “sensitive places”—is correct, but it does not answer Justice Thomas’s more specific objection that Hawaii’s private-property default and expansive location bans may operate as a de facto carry prohibition for ordinary, law-abiding citizens. Under Bruen, the State must produce a well-established, representative analogue matching both the “how” and the “why” of this burden, and generalized invocations of a tradition of regulation are too abstract to sustain a regime that makes public carry largely illusory. Chief Justice Roberts’s institutionalist, minimalist impulse toward a remand keyed to real-world operation is appealing, but unless the record shows meaningful avenues for carry and the State can identify comparably burdensome founding-era restrictions, the Second Amendment claim prevails. I also agree with Roberts (and Kagan) that Rule 702 can assist with historical context and authentication, but courts cannot outsource the analogue analysis or ultimate constitutional meaning to experts.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that Heller and Bruen preserve regulation of manner and genuinely “sensitive places”—is correct, but under Bruen it cannot justify a regime whose design and practical operation make ordinary public carry the exception rather than the rule unless the State identifies a well-established, representative analogue imposing a comparably broad burden for a comparable reason. Justice Jackson’s suggestion of granular, provision-by-provision salvage underscores the right remedial instinct, yet it still presupposes the State can carry its historical burden for each sweeping default rule; on this record, Hawaii relies on generalities rather than concrete analogues matching the “how and why.” I agree with Chief Justice Roberts (and Justice Kagan) that Rule 702 may assist with context and authentication, but not with ultimate constitutional meaning; allowing experts to supply that bottom line would dilute Bruen’s judicial analogue analysis and risk interest-balancing through abstraction. Because the respondents’ historical showing remains too generalized to sustain a broad default prohibition (including the private-property presumption) as enacted and as it functions, I remain with Petitioner.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s “carry nowhere” critique remains the most serious challenge: if the private-property default and location bans, as applied, make ordinary public carry practically impossible, Bruen would not permit the State to evade the right by relabeling most of daily life as off-limits. But Chief Justice Roberts’s minimalist instinct cuts the other way for me on remedy—rather than facially striking the whole regime, courts should test the scheme’s specific components against concrete historical analogues and invalidate only those parts that impose a comparably sweeping burden without representative historical support. Justice Gorsuch is right that judicial narrowing cannot substitute for the State’s burden, yet that point supports targeted invalidation or remand focused on real-world operation and severability, not a conclusion that no portion (e.g., genuinely sensitive places or historically grounded manner rules) can survive. On Rule 702, I agree with Roberts/Kagan/Thomas that historians may provide context and authentication but cannot supply bottom-line constitutional meaning, which reinforces a court-driven, provision-by-provision Bruen analysis rather than an all-or-nothing disposition.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under Bruen, once the Second Amendment’s plain text covers carrying a handgun in public for self-defense, Hawaii bears the burden to justify its restrictions by identifying a “well-established and representative” historical analogue, not by invoking public-safety interest balancing. On this record, Hawaii’s regime—if it effectively makes ordinary public carry broadly unlawful or converts “shall-issue” into practical denial through sweeping location bans or discretionary constraints—resembles the kind of near-prohibition Bruen rejected and is unlikely to be supported by the limited “sensitive places” tradition recognized in Heller and Bruen. Separately, while historians may assist a court in understanding sources, Fed. R. Evid. 702 does not permit party-retained experts to supply ultimate legal conclusions about constitutional meaning; interpretation of founding-era law is for the court, and reliance on expert “legal” opinions risks undermining the judiciary’s institutional role. A narrow disposition would therefore remand with instructions to apply Bruen’s historical-analogue framework rigorously and to cabin expert testimony to factual historical context rather than constitutional conclusions.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Under Bruen, once the Second Amendment’s plain text covers carrying arms in public for self-defense, Hawaii bears the burden to justify its restrictions by identifying a well-established historical analogue from the founding era, not by invoking generalized public-safety rationales or interest balancing. A regime that issues licenses “to carry nowhere” (including by default prohibiting carry on most private property open to the public absent affirmative consent) appears inconsistent with the original public meaning of “bear Arms” recognized in Heller and applied to the States in McDonald. Courts must decide the law, including the meaning of founding-era statutes and constitutional text; party-retained historians may assist with factual context, but under Fed. R. Evid. 702 they may not supply legal conclusions that effectively displace the judicial task of interpreting text and history. Because Hawaii has not shown a sufficiently analogous historical tradition supporting such sweeping public-carry prohibitions, the restrictions violate the Second Amendment.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Under Bruen, once the Second Amendment’s plain text covers carrying arms for self-defense, the State bears the burden to justify its restriction by identifying a well-established historical analogue, not by invoking broad public-safety rationales. Hawaii’s regime, as described, appears to function as a substantial constraint on ordinary public carry, and Bruen rejected similarly discretionary or effectively prohibitory approaches while emphasizing that only narrow, historically grounded “sensitive places” and comparable traditions can justify modern limits. On the evidentiary point, Fed. R. Evid. 702 permits experts to assist with historical facts and context, but courts may not outsource constitutional and statutory interpretation—i.e., ultimate legal conclusions about founding-era meaning—to party-retained historians, because that is the court’s duty. Consistent with Heller and McDonald, the practical consequence of allowing States to evade Bruen’s burden through generalized expert-driven “tradition” assertions would be to dilute a constitutional right into a policy balancing test this Court has foreclosed.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Applying Bruen, the State bears the burden to justify a public-carry restriction by showing it is consistent with this Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation, and history reflects longstanding regulation of the manner and sensitive locations of carrying arms rather than an unlimited right to carry anywhere. Heller itself emphasized the Second Amendment right is “not unlimited” and preserved a wide range of historically grounded regulations, a point Bruen reiterated even as it rejected means-end interest balancing. On the evidentiary question, Fed. R. Evid. 702 permits historians to assist the court with background facts about founding-era practices and sources, but courts must not outsource constitutional meaning or treat expert testimony as binding legal conclusions—interpretation remains the judiciary’s job. Given the substantial public-safety stakes for vulnerable communities and the availability of historically analogous location- and condition-based carry restrictions, Hawaii’s regime should be upheld so long as it is anchored in genuine historical analogues rather than policy alone.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under Bruen, once the Second Amendment’s plain text covers carrying arms for self-defense in public, Hawaii bears the burden to show a well-established historical analogue supporting its restrictions, and generalized public-safety rationales cannot substitute for that historical showing. On this record, Hawaii’s asserted tradition of regulating the “manner, locations, and conditions” of carry is too abstract unless it maps to comparably broad, enduring founding-era limits on ordinary public carry rather than narrow ‘sensitive places’ or unusual-danger regulations recognized in Heller and Bruen. Separately, while historians may assist the court by identifying and contextualizing founding-era sources, Fed. R. Evid. 702 does not permit party-retained experts to offer what are effectively legal conclusions about constitutional meaning or the legal validity of purported analogues—those interpretive judgments remain for the court. Because the State has not carried its Bruen burden with a sufficiently concrete historical analogue (and cannot cure that gap by outsourcing legal interpretation to experts), Hawaii’s regime as applied here violates the Second Amendment.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Under Bruen, once the Second Amendment’s plain text covers the conduct—bearing arms in public for self-defense—the State bears the burden to justify its restriction by demonstrating consistency with the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation, not by invoking generalized public-safety balancing or empirical policy claims. Hawaii’s regime, to the extent it operates as a broad default prohibition on public carry absent discretionary permission or sweeping “sensitive place” expansions, is difficult to reconcile with Heller and Bruen’s recognition that the right to “bear” arms includes ordinary public carry. As to historians offered as Rule 702 experts, courts may receive assistance in identifying and contextualizing historical materials, but constitutional meaning and the selection of proper analogues are legal conclusions reserved to the judiciary, not subjects for party-retained experts to supply. The judgment below should be reversed where it departs from Bruen’s text-and-history methodology and permits expert testimony to substitute for the court’s own legal analysis.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under Bruen, once the Second Amendment’s plain text covers public carry, Hawaii must justify its restrictions by identifying a historical tradition of analogous regulation, focusing on how and why founding-era laws regulated carrying in public. If Hawaii’s regime functions as a near-prohibition on ordinary, law-abiding citizens carrying for self-defense—by broadly designating most places as off-limits or imposing discretionary conditions untethered to historical practice—it likely fails Bruen, but if it resembles historically recognized location- and manner-based limits, it can be sustained consistent with Heller’s acknowledgement that the right is not unlimited. On the evidentiary point, courts may consider historians to illuminate the historical record, but under Fed. R. Evid. 702 they should not accept party-retained experts’ bottom-line constitutional or statutory-interpretive conclusions, because the legal meaning of historical sources is for judges to decide. Given the institutional need for administrable rules and adherence to Bruen’s analogue framework without converting trials into dueling legal-interpretation experts, I would uphold Hawaii’s law as construed to fit within historical location/manner analogues and limit expert testimony to factual historical context.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under Bruen, once the Second Amendment’s plain text covers the proposed conduct—publicly carrying arms for self-defense—the State bears the burden to justify its restriction by identifying a well-established and representative historical analogue, not by appealing to generalized public-safety rationales or means-end balancing. Hawaii’s defense, as framed, relies on broad assertions that governments historically regulated public carry without anchoring the modern regime to sufficiently analogous founding-era (or Reconstruction-era) restrictions of comparable burden and justification, which Bruen rejects. As to historians, courts may consider expert assistance to authenticate sources and provide historical context, but Rule 702 does not permit party-retained experts to offer what amount to legal conclusions about constitutional meaning or the operative rule of decision; that interpretive judgment belongs to the court applying the text-and-history test. Heller and McDonald reinforce that the right to “bear” arms extends beyond the home and cannot be treated as a second-class right subject to free-floating policy justifications.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under Bruen, once the Second Amendment’s text covers public carry, the State bears the burden to justify its restrictions by demonstrating a historical tradition of analogous regulations, and that inquiry must remain a judicial one rather than a policy balancing test. Properly framed, Hawaii may defend at least some location- and manner-based limits on public carry by pointing to historically recognized restrictions on bearing arms in sensitive places and comparable public-safety regulations consistent with Heller’s recognition that the right is not unlimited. On the evidentiary question, Fed. R. Evid. 702 permits historians to supply factual context about founding-era practices, but courts must police the line against experts offering ultimate legal conclusions about constitutional meaning; that limitation is a matter of procedural fairness and preserves the court’s role. Because the State can rely on historically grounded analogues (not empirical interest-balancing) while the court independently performs the legal analysis, I would vote to uphold Hawaii’s regime at least to the extent it is cabined to historically supported restrictions.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Hawaii’s restrictions on carrying firearms in public (including broad location-based bans and related permitting limits) violate the Second Amendment under the text-and-history test announced in Bruen, and whether courts may rely on “expert” testimony that effectively offers legal conclusions about founding-era statutes and Supreme Court holdings.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. II (as incorporated against the States through the Fourteenth Amendment); evidentiary overlay: Fed. R. Evid. 702 (limits on expert testimony offering legal conclusions).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that Hawaii’s carry regime and expansive place-based prohibitions burden conduct covered by the Second Amendment’s plain text (public carry for self-defense) and therefore are presumptively unconstitutional unless the State can prove a well-established historical analogue. They contend Hawaii and lower courts have attempted to evade Heller, McDonald, and especially Bruen by (1) reintroducing interest-balancing under the guise of public-safety policy and empirical claims, which McDonald rejected as a basis to negate the right’s core, and (2) using putative historical “experts” to tell courts how to interpret founding-era laws and to pronounce that key holdings in Heller/McDonald/Bruen are “historically accurate,” which petitioners characterize as impermissible legal conclusions under Rule 702 because statutory and constitutional interpretation is for judges, not expert witnesses.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent (Hawaii) defends its regulatory scheme as consistent with the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation, arguing that the State may impose significant conditions and location-based restrictions on public carry to address safety and sensitive-place concerns while still leaving avenues for lawful armed self-defense. Hawaii also appears to rely on historical evidence and expert submissions to characterize founding-era and later analogues as supporting modern restrictions, contending that courts may consider the historical record compiled by the parties (and may conduct their own research) to determine whether the challenged regulations fit within historically accepted limits on the right.
key_precedents: District of Columbia v. Heller, 554 U.S. 570 (2008)
McDonald v. City of Chicago, 561 U.S. 742 (2010)
New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen, 597 U.S. 1 (2022)
Heller v. District of Columbia (Heller II), 670 F.3d 1244 (D.C. Cir. 2011) (Kavanaugh, J., dissenting) (quoted re: later history vs. text)
Commodores Entertainment Corp. v. McClary, 879 F.3d 1114 (11th Cir. 2018) (statutory interpretation is for the court)
United States v. Herring, 955 F.2d 703 (11th Cir. 1992) (court must guard against expert legal conclusions)
Glenn H. Reynolds & Brannon P. Denning, Heller’s Future in the Lower Courts, 102 Nw. U. L. Rev. 2035 (2008) (commentary on lower-court resistance)

John Roberts.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—pressed by Justice Sotomayor—that Bruen allows analogical reasoning and preserves regulation in genuinely “sensitive places” is correct, but it does not answer Bruen’s limiting principle: sensitive-place logic cannot be aggregated into a functional near-ban that leaves only “bare passage” in ordinary public life. As Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Thomas emphasize, Hawaii still bears the burden to affirmatively prove a well-established, representative historical tradition for each broad category, and the combination of expansive place prohibitions plus a private-property default rule must be evaluated for whether it recreates the “Manhattan-as-sensitive-place” regime Bruen rejected. Justice Kagan’s Rule 702 point supplies an institutionally modest, administrable basis for vacatur and remand: historians may provide historical facts and context, but not legal conclusions about constitutional meaning or what Heller/McDonald/Bruen “hold.” A narrow V&R on those grounds respects precedent and avoids premature, overbroad merits pronouncements while ensuring the lower court applies Bruen’s burden with clear boundaries.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that Bruen permits analogue reasoning and recognizes “sensitive places,” but that latitude cannot be used to convert most ordinary public spaces into gun-free zones, because Bruen expressly rejected expansions that operate like a near-general prohibition on bearing arms. Even accepting a non-“dead ringer” analogue approach, Hawaii still must identify a well-established founding-era tradition for bans of this breadth, and modern public-safety rationales cannot substitute for historical justification under Heller, McDonald, and Bruen. I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that historians may aid with historical facts, but Rule 702 does not allow experts to supply legal conclusions about the meaning of founding-era statutes or what this Court’s precedents “hold,” since that interpretive duty remains with judges. On this record, the State has not carried its burden, and the scheme appears to be precisely the kind of evasion through overbroad “sensitive places” that Bruen forbids.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—pressed most charitably by Justice Sotomayor—is that Bruen allows analogical reasoning and recognizes genuinely “sensitive places,” so Hawaii need not produce a founding-era twin for every modern restriction. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, Bruen’s own limiting principle forbids using that flexibility to label broad swaths of ordinary public life as sensitive and thereby leave citizens only “bare passage,” which looks like the “Manhattan” evasion Bruen rejected. Even granting the State latitude to reason by analogy, it still must affirmatively prove a representative historical tradition supporting restrictions of this combined breadth; generalized public-congregation logic and modern safety rationales do not meet that burden under Bruen’s methodology. I also agree with Justice Kagan that Rule 702 may admit historians for factual context but not legal conclusions about constitutional meaning, and that evidentiary discipline reinforces (rather than cures) the conclusion that the State has not carried its historical showing on this record.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point is that Bruen preserves room for regulation in genuinely “sensitive places” and does not demand a founding-era twin for every modern restriction, but that flexibility has a constitutional ceiling when the combined scheme operates as a near-general prohibition on public carry. Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s “bare passage/Manhattan-as-sensitive-place” limiting principle is decisive for me on this record: Hawaii’s layered location bans plus a default prohibition on private property risk converting the exception into the rule without the “representative” historical tradition Bruen requires. Justice Kagan’s Rule 702 proposal is methodologically useful—historians can supply context while courts decide constitutional meaning—but evidentiary policing cannot cure a scheme whose breadth appears to nullify ordinary public self-defense in practice. The institutionally modest and fair disposition is vacatur and remand for a category-by-category sensitive-places analysis that also accounts for the cumulative effect of the restrictions and demands a tighter historical analogue showing.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The strongest opposing point, pressed by Justice Sotomayor, is that Bruen’s analogical method allows regulation of genuinely “sensitive places” without a founding-era carbon copy; I agree with that premise but it cannot do the work Hawaii asks of it here. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, Bruen’s limiting principle forbids aggregating broad categories of ordinary destinations—plus a private-property default—into a scheme that functionally recreates the near-general public-carry prohibition Bruen rejected (the “Manhattan” problem). No colleague has identified a precedent beyond Heller/McDonald/Bruen that supplies a textual or historical limiting principle capable of validating this breadth, and the Rule 702 point (historians for historical facts, not legal conclusions) reinforces a modest vacate-and-remand to force category-by-category justification and prevent expert-driven dilution of the State’s burden. On this record, the State’s analogies remain too loose and risk collapsing the exception into the rule, so I stay with petitioner.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—pressed by Justice Sotomayor—is that Bruen allows analogical reasoning and preserves regulation in genuinely “sensitive places,” but that does not justify aggregating broad categories plus a private-property default into a regime that leaves only “bare passage,” the very evasion Bruen warned against. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh correctly focus on the limiting principle: sensitive-place bans must be discrete and historically grounded, not a general label for ordinary destinations where people congregate. I also agree with Justice Kagan that Rule 702 may admit historians for factual context, but it cannot outsource constitutional meaning or what Heller/McDonald/Bruen “hold” to experts; courts must do that interpretive work. On this record Hawaii has not affirmatively proved a representative founding-era tradition for restrictions of this combined breadth, so I remain for vacatur (at minimum) and remand under proper Bruen and evidentiary standards.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that Bruen expressly allows historical-analogue reasoning and preserves regulation in genuinely “sensitive places,” so Hawaii need not produce a founding-era twin for every modern location. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas stress, Bruen’s limiting principle forbids using that flexibility to label most ordinary public destinations as sensitive and, combined with a private-property default, reduce lawful carry to “bare passage,” functionally recreating the near-general ban Bruen rejected. I also agree with Justice Kagan that Rule 702 may admit historians for historical facts and context but must exclude testimony that offers legal conclusions about constitutional meaning or what Heller/McDonald/Bruen “hold,” and a vacate-and-remand enforcing both the burden and the evidentiary boundary is the institutionally sound course. On this record, Hawaii has not affirmatively proved a well-established, representative tradition supporting restrictions of this combined breadth.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—pressed most carefully by Justice Sotomayor—is that Bruen allows historical-analogue reasoning and leaves room for regulation in genuinely “sensitive places,” so Hawaii need not find a founding-era “dead ringer” for each modern location. But Bruen’s own limiting principle, which the Chief Justice highlights, forbids aggregating broad, ordinary destinations (plus a private-property default) into a regime that functionally recreates a near-general public-carry ban—the “Manhattan” problem—and the State still bears the burden to affirmatively prove a well-established, representative tradition for restrictions of this combined breadth. I also agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan that Rule 702 must be policed so historians supply historical facts and context rather than legal conclusions about constitutional meaning; that institutional guardrail reinforces, rather than replaces, the conclusion that the present record does not justify restrictions of this sweep. Nothing offered on the respondent’s side supplies a historically grounded limiting principle that prevents “sensitive places” from swallowing the public sphere, so I remain for petitioner and favor vacatur and remand on the Chief’s narrower path.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The strongest point on the other side is Justice Sotomayor’s framework claim that Bruen preserves a meaningful sensitive-places category and permits analogue reasoning without a founding-era “dead ringer,” but that principle does not answer the practical problem this record presents: Hawaii’s broad, layered place bans plus a default prohibition on private property risk making lawful public carry the exception—exactly the sort of functional “Manhattan-as-sensitive-place” evasion Bruen warned against. Chief Justice Roberts’s proposal to vacate and remand is therefore the most procedurally fair and pragmatic course, because it forces the State to carry Bruen’s burden with representative historical analogues for each broad category and requires the lower court to assess the combined effect rather than atomizing restrictions. I also agree with Justice Kagan that Rule 702 can admit historians for historical facts and context, but cannot be used to smuggle in legal conclusions about what Heller/McDonald/Bruen mean, since that would distort the allocation of interpretive responsibility and the State’s burden. Nothing advanced by the respondent supplies a historically grounded limiting principle that prevents “sensitive places” from swallowing ordinary public life, so my vote remains for petitioner.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under Bruen, once petitioners show the Second Amendment’s plain text covers public carry for self-defense, Hawaii must “affirmatively prove” a well-established historical analogue for its broad location-based bans and permitting limits, and Bruen cautions against expanding “sensitive places” by loose analogy into a near-general prohibition that confines carry to “bare passage” on streets and sidewalks. 597 U.S. 1, 24, 31 (2022). If Hawaii’s scheme effectively replicates the “Manhattan-as-sensitive-place” regime Bruen condemned, it cannot be sustained on public-safety interest balancing or isolated, late, or discriminatory outlier laws. On the evidentiary point, Fed. R. Evid. 702 permits historical experts to aid the court on facts (what sources say and how practices existed), but not to offer legal conclusions about the meaning of founding-era statutes or to pronounce what Heller/McDonald/Bruen “hold,” because constitutional and statutory interpretation remains for judges. A narrow disposition would be to vacate and remand for application of Bruen’s sensitive-places limits and for exclusion of expert testimony to the extent it supplies legal conclusions under Rule 702.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Second Amendment’s text protects the right to “bear” arms, and Bruen held that this includes carrying handguns in public for self-defense and that any restriction is presumptively unlawful unless the State proves a well-established historical analogue consistent with the founding-era tradition. Hawaii’s broad location-based bans and permitting limits appear to function as a near-general prohibition on public carry, which Bruen rejected as an evasion via “sensitive places” expansions and interest-balancing based on public-safety policy. Under Heller and McDonald, courts may not dilute the right’s core by weighing costs and benefits, and under Fed. R. Evid. 702 (as reflected in decisions like Herring and Commodores), courts should not outsource legal interpretation of historical statutes or Supreme Court holdings to “experts” offering legal conclusions. Because the State bears the historical burden and cannot satisfy it through policy empirics or expert legal conclusions, the restrictions violate the Second Amendment as incorporated by the Fourteenth.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Under Bruen, once petitioners show that public carry for self-defense is covered by the Second Amendment’s plain text, Hawaii must justify broad location-based bans and permitting limits by identifying a well-established historical analogue, not by reciting modern public-safety interests or empirical policy judgments.
